# **How did the Cincinnati Reds do in the 2026 regular season?**

How many games did they play, how many did they win, and when did they play them? You'll make a request, turn what comes back into a table, and then check whether the table says what you think it says.

A few things:

1.  Add `#| echo: false` to your code blocks.
2.  Use a new block when you move to a new task.
3.  Code goes in the blocks. **Answers go outside them**, as prose. A comment inside a code chunk is not an answer.
4.  Save the raw response to a file **once**, then work from the file. You'll see why in Part 1.

Due Monday at 8pm.

# Part 1: Ask

## The request

These parameters will get you the Reds' 2026 regular season:

| parameter  | value  | meaning               |
|------------|--------|-----------------------|
| `sportId`  | `1`    | Major League Baseball |
| `teamId`   | `113`  | Cincinnati Reds       |
| `season`   | `2026` |                       |
| `gameType` | `R`    | regular season        |

Build the request, send it, and check the status.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| echo: false
reds_request <- request("https://statsapi.mlb.com/api/v1/schedule") |>
  req_url_query(sportId = 1, teamId = 113, season = 2026, gameType = "R")
reds_request |> req_dry_run()
reds_response <- reds_request |> req_perform()
resp_status(reds_response)
resp_url(reds_response)
```

## Read the fine print

The first field in every response is `copyright`.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| echo: false
library(tidyverse)
library(httr2)

```

> What does it say? Follow the link it gives you. What kinds of use does MLB permit? "The accounts, descriptions, data and presentation in the referring page (the "Materials") are proprietary content of MLB Advanced Media, L.P ("MLBAM"). Only individual, non-commercial, non-bulk use of the Materials is permitted and any other use of the Materials is prohibited without prior written authorization from MLBAM. Authorized users of the Materials are prohibited from using the Materials in any commercial manner other than as expressly authorized by MLBAM."

> Is this assignment a permitted use? Would it still be if all 25 of us wrote a loop that requested every game of every season? Explain. Yes, but if we were doing loops that would be bulk so it would not be permitted.

## Save it, then work from the file

Save the raw response to `data/raw/reds_2026.json`. Then read it back in with `jsonlite::read_json()` and use **that** for the rest of the assignment. Put the saving and the reading in **separate** blocks. Once the file is saved, add `#| eval: false` to every block that sends a request **and** to the block that saves, so rendering reads your file instead of asking MLB again.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| echo: false
#| eval: false
request("https://statsapi.mlb.com/api/v1/schedule") |>
  req_url_query(sportId = 1, teamId = 113, season = 2026, gameType = "R") |> 
  req_perform(path = "data/raw/reds_2026.json")

reds_json <- jsonlite::read_json("data/raw/reds_2026.json")
```

> Why work from the file instead of sending the request every time you render? Give two reasons.
>
> Working from a saved file avoids repeatedly requesting the same data from MLB's server, and it makes the analysis reproducible because the data will not unexpectedly change between renders.

> Fill this in:
>
> - URL:
>
>   ```         
>   https://statsapi.mlb.com/api/v1/schedule?sportId=1&teamId=113&season=2026&gameType=R
>   ```
>
> - Date and time requested:
>
>   10/26 9:00 PM
>
> - Status:
>
>   200 OK

> If you ran this same request in March 2027, would you get exactly the same file? What might change?
>
> Running the request again in March 2027 might produce a different file because MLB can correct scores, update game status, or change metadata even after the season ends.

# Part 2: Make it a table

## Look before you reshape

Use `str()` the way we did in class: look at one date, then one game inside it.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| echo: false
#| eval: false
str(reds_json$dates[[1]], max.level = 2)
str(reds_json$dates[[1]]$games[[1]], max.level = 3)
```

> Which parts are `[ ]` (lists of things, which become rows) and which are `{ }` (named things, which become columns)? Write the path from the top of the response down to the Reds' score in one game.
>
> The dates field is an array of date entries \[ \], and each date has a games list \[ \]. Individual dates, games, teams, and status objects are named objects { }. A path to the Reds' score is dates -\> games -\> teams -\> home -\> score when the Reds are home, or dates -\> games -\> teams -\> away -\> score when the Reds are away. We identify which side is Cincinnati using team ID 113.

## Rectangle it

Create a tibble called `reds` with **one row per entry in `games`** and these columns:

- `game_pk` (`gamePk`)
- `game_date` (`gameDate`)
- `official_date` (`officialDate`)
- `status` (`status` to `detailedState`)
- `home_id`, `away_id` (the team ids)
- `home_score`, `away_score`

Start from `tibble(day = sched$dates)`. In class, `features` was one list of earthquakes. Here, games are a list **inside** a list of dates. How many times will you need `unnest_longer()`? Once you're at one row per game, `hoist()` works the way it did in class.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| echo: false
#| eval: false
str(reds_json$dates[[1]], max.level = 1)
reds <- tibble(day = reds_json$dates)
reds
reds |> 
  unnest_longer(day)
reds_games <- reds |> hoist(day,
                            games = "games") |> 
  select(games) |> 
  unnest_longer(games) |> 
  hoist(games,
        status = c("status", "detailedState"),
        game_pk = "gamePk",
        game_date = "gameDate",
        official_date = "officialDate",
        teams = "teams") |> 
  hoist(teams,
        home = "home",
        away = "away") |>
  hoist(home, home_id = c("team", "id"), home_score = "score") |>
  hoist(away, away_id = c("team", "id"), away_score = "score") |>
  select(game_pk, game_date, official_date, status,
         home_id, away_id, home_score, away_score)

reds_games
reds_json$totalGames
```

> How many rows does `reds` have? What does `totalGames` say? 165. 165.

> A Major League regular season is 162 games. What's going on? A postponed or rescheduled game can have more than one entry.

# Part 3: What is one row?

## Check the key

`gamePk` is MLB's id for a game.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| echo: false
n_distinct(reds_games$game_pk)
repeated_ids <- reds_games |>
  count(game_pk) |>
  filter(n > 1)
repeated_ids
reds_games |>
  semi_join(repeated_ids, by = "game_pk") |>
  arrange(game_pk, official_date)
```

> How many distinct `game_pk` values are there? Which ones appear more than once? 162.
>
> |        |     |     |     |     |
> |-------:|----:|-----|-----|-----|
> | 824490 |   2 |     |     |     |
> | 824514 |   2 |     |     |     |
> | 824518 |   2 |     |     |     |

> Look at every row for those games, alongside their other columns. What happened to them? They were postponed.

> Hint: you might want to use a filtering join :)

## Fix the grain

You want one row per game that was actually played. Use `distinct(game_pk, .keep_all = TRUE)` below.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| echo: false
reds_first <- reds_games |>
  distinct(game_pk, .keep_all = TRUE)
reds_first |>
  semi_join(repeated_ids, by = "game_pk")
```

> For the games that appeared twice, which row did `distinct()` keep? Look at the scores. Is that the row you wanted? Kept the postponed games which do not have scores so it is not the row we want.

> Fix it. Show that your result has one row per `game_pk` and that every row has a score.

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| echo: false
reds_played <- reds_games |>
  filter(!is.na(home_score), !is.na(away_score)) |>
  distinct(game_pk, .keep_all = TRUE)
reds_played |>
  summarise(rows = n(),
            distinct_ids = n_distinct(game_pk),
            missing_home = sum(is.na(home_score)),
            missing_away = sum(is.na(away_score)))
reds_played |>
  semi_join(repeated_ids, by = "game_pk")

reds_results <- reds_played |>
  mutate(reds_score = if_else(home_id == 113, home_score, away_score),
         other_score = if_else(home_id == 113, away_score, home_score),
         result = case_when(
           reds_score > other_score ~ "Win",
           reds_score < other_score ~ "Loss",
           TRUE ~ "Tie"))
reds_results |> count(result)
```

# Part 4: When did they play?

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| echo: false
reds_dates <- reds_results |>
  mutate(game_datetime = as.POSIXct(game_date,
                                    format = "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ",
                                    tz = "UTC"),
         utc_date = as.Date(game_datetime, tz = "UTC"),
         official_day = as.Date(official_date),
         different_date = utc_date != official_day)
reds_dates |> count(different_date)
reds_dates |>
  filter(different_date) |>
  select(game_pk, game_date, official_date, home_id, away_id) 

utc_weekdays <- reds_dates |>
  mutate(weekday = weekdays(utc_date)) |>
  count(weekday, name = "utc_games")
official_weekdays <- reds_dates |>
  mutate(weekday = weekdays(official_day)) |>
  count(weekday, name = "official_games")
utc_weekdays
official_weekdays
utc_weekdays |>
  full_join(official_weekdays, by = "weekday")
```

> Parse `game_date`. What time zone is it in? How do you know? UTC, the Z at the end.

> For how many games does the **date** part of `game_date` differ from `official_date`? Look at a few. What do they have in common? Evening games can be seen as the next day because of the time difference between UTC and the local timezone of the game.

> Count the Reds' games by day of the week twice: once using `game_date` and once using `official_date`. Do you get the same counts? Which one answers "what day did they play?" No. official_date answers the question.

> **Optional:** Convert `game_date` to `America/New_York`. Does that make it agree with `official_date`? Would Eastern time be the right choice for a Reds game played in San Diego?
